FACT_ID: sec02-F01 | anchor: A01
Traffic signs tell you the laws, hazards, places, directions, and services around you, and each sign's shape and color hint at what kind it is [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F02 | anchor: A01
Red means stop, yield, or obey whatever the sign shows [A01].
Why it matters: red is the only color tied to stop and yield commands.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F03 | anchor: A01
Green gives direction, naming a place or how far away it lies [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F04 | anchor: A01
Blue points travelers to services such as rest areas, hospitals, lodging, fuel, food, and attractions [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F05 | anchor: A01
Yellow signals a general warning to slow down and stay alert [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F06 | anchor: A01
Fluorescent yellow-green marks pedestrian, bicycle, and school warning signs [A01].
Why it matters: school-zone warnings use this color, not plain yellow.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F07 | anchor: A01
White carries regulatory messages about enforceable laws and ordinances [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F08 | anchor: A01
Orange warns of road work and temporary traffic control, so watch for changing speed limits and workers on the road [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F09 | anchor: A01
Brown guides you to recreation and cultural points of interest such as parks and historic sites [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F10 | anchor: A01
Fluorescent pink marks incident-management warnings and guides for crash cleanup, debris removal, and traffic control [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0006]

FACT_ID: sec02-F11 | anchor: A02
The eight-sided octagon belongs to the stop sign alone, and you must come to a full stop where it controls the intersection [A02].
Why it matters: shape alone identifies a stop; no other sign may use the octagon.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F12 | anchor: A02
The triangle-shaped sign means you must yield the right of way [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F13 | anchor: A02
Rectangles serve as regulatory, guide, and warning signs [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F14 | anchor: A02
The pennant hangs on the left side of the road and warns you that passing is prohibited ahead [A02].
Why it matters: side placement is part of the meaning; a left-side triangle always means no passing.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F15 | anchor: A02
The diamond warns of special road hazards, and its words or pictures tell you why to slow down or take extra care [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F16 | anchor: A02
A circular sign tells you a railroad crossing lies ahead [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F17 | anchor: A02
The five-sided pentagon marks school areas and school crossings [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

FACT_ID: sec02-F18 | anchor: A02
Crossbuck signs stand at each railroad crossing, and the number plate beneath them tells how many sets of tracks you must cross [A02].
Why it matters: the plate count, not the crossbuck itself, tells you how many track sets to expect.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0007]

Misconceptions: yellow means general warning, but school and pedestrian warnings use fluorescent yellow-green instead; the circle warns that rails lie ahead while the crossbuck marks the crossing itself; the pennant hangs on the left, never on the right.

Mnemonic: red octagon, eight sides, full stop; triangle yields; circle means rails ahead; pentagon protects pupils.

Glossary: regulatory (an enforceable rule sign, usually white); warning (a hazard alert, usually yellow or fluorescent); guide (direction or information); crossbuck (the crossed-boards rail crossing marker); pennant (the sideways triangle for no-passing zones).

Dynamic facts: none in these pages; every color and shape rule above is stable handbook knowledge with no date-variable or place-variable values.
